3 Introducding ggplot2
ggplot2, part of the tidyverse family, is designed based on the Grammar of Graphics for visual exploration and communication.

3.1 R Graphics VS ggplot2
The following histograms demonstrate the outputs by using functions from Base R and ggplot2.


R Graphics
ggplot2




hist(exam_data$MATHS)










ggplot(data = exam_data, aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 10,
                 boundary = 100,
                 colour = "black",
                 fill = "grey") +
  ggtitle("Distribution of Maths Scores")
















Important



As noted by the founder of the tidyverse, Hadley Wickham, even beginners should learn the more advanced ways of using ggplot2. This helps them understand how visualisations are constructed and how data columns or variables are mapped to geometric objects to convey meaningful information.

title: 01: A Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot2 methods
text:
4 Grammar of Graphics
Before using ggplot2, it is important to understand the Grammar of Graphics.
The Grammar of Graphics is a framework for data visualisation that breaks graphs into components such as layers and scales. Introduced by Leland Wilkinson in 1999, it defines rules for combining mathematical and aesthetic elements to create meaningful statistical graphics.
Its key ideas are that graphics are built from layered elements and that meaning is conveyed through aesthetic mapping. This framework helps us understand complex plots and recognise well-formed graphics, though not all grammatically correct plots are necessarily meaningful.

4.1 A Layered Grammar of Graphics
ggplot2 implements Leland Wilkinson’s Grammar of Graphics and is built on seven key components (Wickham, 2010).


Data is the dataset being plotted.

Aesthetics map data variables to visual properties such as position, colour, and size.

Geometrics define how data are displayed, for example points, bars, or lines.

Facets split data into subsets to create multiple panels.

Statistics apply data transformations such as means or confidence intervals.

Coordinate systems control how data are positioned in the plot.

Themes adjust non-data elements such as titles, axes, and legends.

section: 5 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: data
text:
5 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: data
The code chunk below creates a blank canvas by initialising a ggplot object with the data argument. Here, exam_data is used for plotting. If the dataset is not a data.frame, it will be converted automatically and internally using fortify().

ggplot(data=exam_data)

title: 01: A Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot2 methods
section: 6 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: aes()
text:
6 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: aes()
Aesthetic mappings use data attributes to control visual properties such as position, colour, size, shape, and transparency.
All aesthetics are defined using the aes() function, and each geom layer can have its own mappings. The code chunk below adds x-axis and its label to the plot.

ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x=MATHS))

title: 01: A Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot2 methods
section: 7 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: geom()
text:
7 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: geom()
Geometric objects define the actual marks drawn on a plot. Common examples include: - geom_point() for points, - geom_line() for lines, - geom_smooth for trend lines, - geom_bar for bar charts, - geom_histogram() for histograms, - geom_polygon() for shapes, - geom_map() for map-based polygons, - geom_col() for bar charts where the height of each bar comes directly from the variable, - geom_boxplot() for box plot - geom_density() for kernel density estimate(KDE) - geom_abline() geom_hline() geom_vline() for horizontal, vertical, and diagonal reference lines

7.1 Geometric Objects: geom_bar() & geom_col()

ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x=RACE)) + geom_bar()








avg_english <- exam_data %>%
  group_by(RACE) %>%
  summarize(avg_english = mean(ENGLISH, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(RACE = as.factor(RACE))  
ggplot(avg_english, aes(x = RACE, y = avg_english, fill=RACE, alpha = 0.5)) + geom_col()








7.2 Geometric Objects: geom_dotplot()
In a dot plot, the width of each dot reflects the bin width, and dots are stacked so that each dot represents one observation. The plot created by using geom_dotplot() has a misleading y-axis.

ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x=MATHS)) + 
  geom_dotplot(dotsize=0.5)







The scale_y_continuous() function removes the usefulness of the y-axis. Additionally, scale_x_continuous() is used for numeric data, while scale_x_discrete() or scale_y_discrete() are used for categorical data.

ggplot(data = exam_data, aes(x=MATHS)) + 
  geom_dotplot(binwidth = 2.5, dotsize = 0.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, # remove the y-axis label
                     breaks = NULL) #remove the y-axis tick marks and scale








7.3 Geometric Objects: geom_histogram()

The code chunk below creates a histogram of Maths scores with default bin width 30.

ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x=MATHS)) +geom_histogram()








7.4 Modifying a Geometric Object by Changing geom()
In the code chunk below, the bins argument sets the number of bins to 20, the fill argument shades the histogram in light blue, and the colour argument changes the bar outlines to black.

ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x=MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "lightblue", colour = "black")








7.5 Modifying a Geometric Object by Changing aes()
Yes, it is similar to hue in Python (for example in seaborn).
In ggplot2, mapping fill, alpha, colour inside aes() splits the data into subgroups and assigns different colours to each group. This works in a similar way to hue (seaborn Python), which colours plots based on a categorical variable.

ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x=MATHS, 
                           fill = GENDER, colour = GENDER)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, colour = "gray30") #setting colour in geom will override the ourline colours in aes()








ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x=MATHS, 
                           fill = GENDER, colour = GENDER, alpha = GENDER)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20) #setting colour in geom will override the ourline colours in aes()








7.6 Geometric Objects: geom-density()
geom_density() plots a kernel density estimate, which is a smooth alternative to a histogram for continuous data. The code below displays the distribution of Maths scores using a density plot.

ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x=MATHS)) +
  geom_density()







The code chunk below plots two kernel density curves by mapping colour or fill within aes().

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS, fill= GENDER)) +
  geom_density()








ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS,
           colour = GENDER)) +
  geom_density()








7.7 Geometric Objects: geom_boxplot()

A boxplot summarises the distribution of MATHS scores by GENDER, which is categorical on the x-axis.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(y = MATHS,       
           x= GENDER)) +    
  geom_boxplot()







The code below shows a notched plot of Maths scores by gender. Notches in box plots help compare medians across groups. If the notches do not overlap, it suggests the medians are different.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(y = MATHS, 
           x= GENDER)) +
  geom_boxplot(notch=TRUE)







geom_line() is designed to connect points along a continuous or ordered x-axis. Here, GENDER is categorical, so drawing lines across it has no meaningful interpretation.
Mapping group = RACE forces ggplot2 to connect observations of the same race across gender categories, which results in arbitrary zig-zag lines that do not represent a valid trend.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(y = MATHS,       
           x= GENDER)) +    
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_line(aes(group = RACE), colour = "#3366FF", alpha = 0.5)








7.8 Geometric Objects: geom_violin()

geom_violin() creates violin plots for comparing multiple data distributions. By placing distributions side by side, it makes comparisons easier than overlapping density curves. The code below shows the distribution of Maths scores by gender using a violin plot.
In a violin plot, stat = “ydensity” controls how the shape of the violin is calculated, based on the distribution of the data along the y-axis.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(y = MATHS, 
           x= GENDER,colour= GENDER)) +
  geom_violin()








7.9 Geometric Objects: geom_point()
geom_point() used to create scatterplot.

ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x=MATHS, y=ENGLISH)) +
geom_point() +
geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "blue")








7.10 geom objects can be combined
The code chunk below plots the data points on the boxplots by using both geom_boxplot() and geom_point().

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(y = MATHS, 
           x= GENDER)) +
  geom_boxplot() +                    
  geom_point(position="jitter", 
             size = 0.5)        







geom_point(position = "identity") plots all points at the exact same x-position for each gender category. Since GENDER is categorical, many points overlap completely. position = "identity" is suitable for continuous x-values. For categorical x-values, we should use jitter to avoid overplotting like the example above.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(y = MATHS, 
           x= GENDER)) +
  geom_boxplot() +                    
  geom_point(position="identity", 
             size = 0.5)

section: 8 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: stat()
text:
8 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: stat()
Statistical functions summarise or transform data, such as means, or confidence limits in a bar chart. They can be used by adding a stat_() function and overriding the default geom, or by adding a geom_() function and overriding the default stat.

8.1 Working with stat()
The plot does not display the means by default.

ggplot(data = exam_data, aes(y = MATHS, x = GENDER)) +
  geom_boxplot()








8.2 Working with stat: the stat_summary() method
The code below uses the fun argument to specify the “mean” and displays it as a “point” via the geom argument, with its size and colour set in stat_summary(). Some common geoms are “point”, “line”, “area”, “bar” and “ploygon”.

ggplot(data = exam_data, aes(x=GENDER, y = MATHS)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  stat_summary(geom = "point",
               fun = "mean",
               colour = "red",
               size = 4)








8.3 Working with stat: the geom() method
The code chunk below demonstrates the alternative approach using geom_point(). The point shape can be specified using integer numbers from 0 to 25, or by using single alphanumeric characters. fill argument can also be utilised under geom_point().

ggplot(data= exam_data,
       aes(y=MATHS, x=GENDER)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(stat = "summary",
             fun = "mean",
             colour = "red",
             size = 6,
             shape = "*")








8.4 Adding a Best Fit Curve on a Scatterplot
The code below adds a best fit curve on the catterplot for Maths/English scores by adding a geom_smooth() with the method “loess” that stands for Local Polynomial Regression Fitting and used for observations less than 1k.

ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x=MATHS, y=ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point() + geom_smooth(linewidth=0.5)







The other smoothing methods include “lm”, “glm”, “gam” etc. The chart below is smoothed using a linear regression model based on y ~ x.

ggplot(data = exam_data, aes(x=MATHS, y=ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = lm, linewidth= 0.5)

title: 01: A Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot2 methods
section: 9 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: Facets
text:
9 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: Facets
Faceting creates small multiple plots, or trellis plots, where each panel shows a subset of the data. In ggplot2, this is done using facet_grid() or facet_wrap() to display multiple plots together.

9.1 Working with facet_wrap()
facet_wrap() converts a one-dimensional set of panels into a two-dimensional layout, which typically uses screen space more efficiently. The code below demonstrates a trellis plot created with facet_wrap().

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x= MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20) +
    facet_wrap(~ CLASS)








9.2 Working with facet_grid()
facet_grid() arranges panels in a matrix defined by row and column faceting variables. It works best when there are two discrete variables and all their combinations appear in the data.

ggplot(data= exam_data, aes(x=MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=30) +
  facet_grid(~ GENDER)

title: 01: A Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot2 methods
section: 10 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: Coordinates
text:
10 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: Coordinates
The coordinate functions determine how data values are translated into positions on the plotting plane. ggplot2 provides several coordinate systems, each suited to different visual needs. The main ones are:

coord_cartesian(): the default Cartesian coordinate system, where you specify x and y values (e.g. allows you to zoom in or out).
coord_flip(): a Cartesian system with the x and y flipped.
coord_fixed(): a Cartesian system with a “fixed” aspect ratio (e.g. 1.78 for a “widescreen” plot).
coord_quickmap(): a coordinate system that approximates a good aspect ratio for maps.


10.1 Working with Coordinates
By default, a bar chart is displayed with the x-axis on the horizontal direction and the bars extending vertically upward, as shown in the example below.

ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x=RACE)) + geom_bar()







The code chunk below flips the x-axis to y-axis.

ggplot(exam_data, aes(x=RACE)) + geom_bar() + coord_flip()








10.2 Chaning the y-axis and x-axis Range
The scatterplot appears slightly off-centre because the axes start at different minimum values. In this case, the y-axis starts at 20, while the x-axis starts at 0, so the plotting area is not symmetric around the origin.
This happens when ggplot2 automatically sets axis limits based on the range of the data rather than forcing both axes to start at the same value. As a result, the visual centre of the plot shifts, even though the data points themselves are correctly positioned.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x= MATHS, y=ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method=lm, size=0.5)







coord_cartesian() function is used to realign the axes so they starting from 0 to 100.

ggplot(exam_data, aes(x=MATHS, y=ENGLISH)) +
        geom_point() +
        geom_smooth(method=lm, size = 0.5) +
        coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0,100), ylim= c(0,100))







Adding an additional coordinate system replaces the existing one.

ggplot(exam_data, aes(x=MATHS, y=ENGLISH)) +
        geom_point() +
        geom_smooth(method=lm, size = 0.5) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0,100), ylim= c(0,100)) +
        coord_fixed(ratio=1.78)

title: 01: A Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot2 methods
section: 11 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: themes
text:
11 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: themes
Themes control the appearance of a graph rather than the data itself, such as background colour, fonts, gridlines, and label colours.
ggplot2 includes built in themes like theme_grey() (default), theme_bw(), and theme_classic(). Theme elements are grouped into lines, rectangles, and text.

11.1 Working wth themes
theme_grey() is the default theme with background colour in grey.

ggplot(exam_data, aes(x=RACE, fill=RACE, alpha=0.5)) +
  geom_bar() +
  coord_flip() + 
  theme_grey()







The colour theme could be changed to classic where background in white and gridlines removed by using theme_classic().

ggplot(exam_data, aes(x=RACE,fill = GENDER, alpha=0.5)) + 
  geom_bar() +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_classic()







Or the theme can be set to minimal.

ggplot(exam_data, aes(x=RACE, fill=CLASS, alpha = 0.5)) + 
  geom_bar() +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal()







Or the theme can be set to light.

ggplot(exam_data, aes(x=RACE,fill=CLASS, alpha = 0.5)) + 
  geom_bar() +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_light()







Or the theme can be set to test.

ggplot(exam_data, aes(x=RACE,fill=CLASS)) + 
  geom_bar(alpha=0.5) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette="Paired")






  theme_test()

3 Introducding ggplot2
ggplot2, part of the tidyverse family, is designed based on the Grammar of Graphics for visual exploration and communication.

3.1 R Graphics VS ggplot2
The following histograms demonstrate the outputs by using functions from Base R and ggplot2.


R Graphics
ggplot2




hist(exam_data$MATHS)










ggplot(data = exam_data, aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 10,
                 boundary = 100,
                 colour = "black",
                 fill = "grey") +
  ggtitle("Distribution of Maths Scores")
















Important



As noted by the founder of the tidyverse, Hadley Wickham, even beginners should learn the more advanced ways of using ggplot2. This helps them understand how visualisations are constructed and how data columns or variables are mapped to geometric objects to convey meaningful information.

title: 01: A Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot2 methods
text:
4 Grammar of Graphics
Before using ggplot2, it is important to understand the Grammar of Graphics.
The Grammar of Graphics is a framework for data visualisation that breaks graphs into components such as layers and scales. Introduced by Leland Wilkinson in 1999, it defines rules for combining mathematical and aesthetic elements to create meaningful statistical graphics.
Its key ideas are that graphics are built from layered elements and that meaning is conveyed through aesthetic mapping. This framework helps us understand complex plots and recognise well-formed graphics, though not all grammatically correct plots are necessarily meaningful.

4.1 A Layered Grammar of Graphics
ggplot2 implements Leland Wilkinson’s Grammar of Graphics and is built on seven key components (Wickham, 2010).


Data is the dataset being plotted.

Aesthetics map data variables to visual properties such as position, colour, and size.

Geometrics define how data are displayed, for example points, bars, or lines.

Facets split data into subsets to create multiple panels.

Statistics apply data transformations such as means or confidence intervals.

Coordinate systems control how data are positioned in the plot.

Themes adjust non-data elements such as titles, axes, and legends.

title: 01: A Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot2 methods
section: 5 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: data
text:
5 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: data
The code chunk below creates a blank canvas by initialising a ggplot object with the data argument. Here, exam_data is used for plotting. If the dataset is not a data.frame, it will be converted automatically and internally using fortify().

ggplot(data=exam_data)

title: 01: A Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot2 methods
section: 6 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: aes()
text:
6 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: aes()
Aesthetic mappings use data attributes to control visual properties such as position, colour, size, shape, and transparency.
All aesthetics are defined using the aes() function, and each geom layer can have its own mappings. The code chunk below adds x-axis and its label to the plot.

ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x=MATHS))

title: 01: A Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot2 methods
section: 7 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: geom()
text:
7 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: geom()
Geometric objects define the actual marks drawn on a plot. Common examples include: - geom_point() for points, - geom_line() for lines, - geom_smooth for trend lines, - geom_bar for bar charts, - geom_histogram() for histograms, - geom_polygon() for shapes, - geom_map() for map-based polygons, - geom_col() for bar charts where the height of each bar comes directly from the variable, - geom_boxplot() for box plot - geom_density() for kernel density estimate(KDE) - geom_abline() geom_hline() geom_vline() for horizontal, vertical, and diagonal reference lines

7.1 Geometric Objects: geom_bar() & geom_col()

ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x=RACE)) + geom_bar()








avg_english <- exam_data %>%
  group_by(RACE) %>%
  summarize(avg_english = mean(ENGLISH, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(RACE = as.factor(RACE))  
ggplot(avg_english, aes(x = RACE, y = avg_english, fill=RACE, alpha = 0.5)) + geom_col()








7.2 Geometric Objects: geom_dotplot()
In a dot plot, the width of each dot reflects the bin width, and dots are stacked so that each dot represents one observation. The plot created by using geom_dotplot() has a misleading y-axis.

ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x=MATHS)) + 
  geom_dotplot(dotsize=0.5)







The scale_y_continuous() function removes the usefulness of the y-axis. Additionally, scale_x_continuous() is used for numeric data, while scale_x_discrete() or scale_y_discrete() are used for categorical data.

ggplot(data = exam_data, aes(x=MATHS)) + 
  geom_dotplot(binwidth = 2.5, dotsize = 0.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, # remove the y-axis label
                     breaks = NULL) #remove the y-axis tick marks and scale








7.3 Geometric Objects: geom_histogram()

The code chunk below creates a histogram of Maths scores with default bin width 30.

ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x=MATHS)) +geom_histogram()








7.4 Modifying a Geometric Object by Changing geom()
In the code chunk below, the bins argument sets the number of bins to 20, the fill argument shades the histogram in light blue, and the colour argument changes the bar outlines to black.

ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x=MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "lightblue", colour = "black")








7.5 Modifying a Geometric Object by Changing aes()
Yes, it is similar to hue in Python (for example in seaborn).
In ggplot2, mapping fill, alpha, colour inside aes() splits the data into subgroups and assigns different colours to each group. This works in a similar way to hue (seaborn Python), which colours plots based on a categorical variable.

ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x=MATHS, 
                           fill = GENDER, colour = GENDER)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, colour = "gray30") #setting colour in geom will override the ourline colours in aes()








ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x=MATHS, 
                           fill = GENDER, colour = GENDER, alpha = GENDER)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20) #setting colour in geom will override the ourline colours in aes()








7.6 Geometric Objects: geom-density()
geom_density() plots a kernel density estimate, which is a smooth alternative to a histogram for continuous data. The code below displays the distribution of Maths scores using a density plot.

ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x=MATHS)) +
  geom_density()







The code chunk below plots two kernel density curves by mapping colour or fill within aes().

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS, fill= GENDER)) +
  geom_density()








ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS,
           colour = GENDER)) +
  geom_density()








7.7 Geometric Objects: geom_boxplot()

A boxplot summarises the distribution of MATHS scores by GENDER, which is categorical on the x-axis.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(y = MATHS,       
           x= GENDER)) +    
  geom_boxplot()







The code below shows a notched plot of Maths scores by gender. Notches in box plots help compare medians across groups. If the notches do not overlap, it suggests the medians are different.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(y = MATHS, 
           x= GENDER)) +
  geom_boxplot(notch=TRUE)







geom_line() is designed to connect points along a continuous or ordered x-axis. Here, GENDER is categorical, so drawing lines across it has no meaningful interpretation.
Mapping group = RACE forces ggplot2 to connect observations of the same race across gender categories, which results in arbitrary zig-zag lines that do not represent a valid trend.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(y = MATHS,       
           x= GENDER)) +    
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_line(aes(group = RACE), colour = "#3366FF", alpha = 0.5)








7.8 Geometric Objects: geom_violin()

geom_violin() creates violin plots for comparing multiple data distributions. By placing distributions side by side, it makes comparisons easier than overlapping density curves. The code below shows the distribution of Maths scores by gender using a violin plot.
In a violin plot, stat = “ydensity” controls how the shape of the violin is calculated, based on the distribution of the data along the y-axis.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(y = MATHS, 
           x= GENDER,colour= GENDER)) +
  geom_violin()








7.9 Geometric Objects: geom_point()
geom_point() used to create scatterplot.

ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x=MATHS, y=ENGLISH)) +
geom_point() +
geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "blue")








7.10 geom objects can be combined
The code chunk below plots the data points on the boxplots by using both geom_boxplot() and geom_point().

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(y = MATHS, 
           x= GENDER)) +
  geom_boxplot() +                    
  geom_point(position="jitter", 
             size = 0.5)        







geom_point(position = "identity") plots all points at the exact same x-position for each gender category. Since GENDER is categorical, many points overlap completely. position = "identity" is suitable for continuous x-values. For categorical x-values, we should use jitter to avoid overplotting like the example above.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(y = MATHS, 
           x= GENDER)) +
  geom_boxplot() +                    
  geom_point(position="identity", 
             size = 0.5)

title: 01: A Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot2 methods
section: 8 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: stat()
text:
8 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: stat()
Statistical functions summarise or transform data, such as means, or confidence limits in a bar chart. They can be used by adding a stat_() function and overriding the default geom, or by adding a geom_() function and overriding the default stat.

8.1 Working with stat()
The plot does not display the means by default.

ggplot(data = exam_data, aes(y = MATHS, x = GENDER)) +
  geom_boxplot()








8.2 Working with stat: the stat_summary() method
The code below uses the fun argument to specify the “mean” and displays it as a “point” via the geom argument, with its size and colour set in stat_summary(). Some common geoms are “point”, “line”, “area”, “bar” and “ploygon”.

ggplot(data = exam_data, aes(x=GENDER, y = MATHS)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  stat_summary(geom = "point",
               fun = "mean",
               colour = "red",
               size = 4)








8.3 Working with stat: the geom() method
The code chunk below demonstrates the alternative approach using geom_point(). The point shape can be specified using integer numbers from 0 to 25, or by using single alphanumeric characters. fill argument can also be utilised under geom_point().

ggplot(data= exam_data,
       aes(y=MATHS, x=GENDER)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(stat = "summary",
             fun = "mean",
             colour = "red",
             size = 6,
             shape = "*")








8.4 Adding a Best Fit Curve on a Scatterplot
The code below adds a best fit curve on the catterplot for Maths/English scores by adding a geom_smooth() with the method “loess” that stands for Local Polynomial Regression Fitting and used for observations less than 1k.

ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x=MATHS, y=ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point() + geom_smooth(linewidth=0.5)







The other smoothing methods include “lm”, “glm”, “gam” etc. The chart below is smoothed using a linear regression model based on y ~ x.

ggplot(data = exam_data, aes(x=MATHS, y=ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = lm, linewidth= 0.5)

title: 01: A Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot2 methods
section: 9 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: Facets
text:
9 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: Facets
Faceting creates small multiple plots, or trellis plots, where each panel shows a subset of the data. In ggplot2, this is done using facet_grid() or facet_wrap() to display multiple plots together.

9.1 Working with facet_wrap()
facet_wrap() converts a one-dimensional set of panels into a two-dimensional layout, which typically uses screen space more efficiently. The code below demonstrates a trellis plot created with facet_wrap().

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x= MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20) +
    facet_wrap(~ CLASS)








9.2 Working with facet_grid()
facet_grid() arranges panels in a matrix defined by row and column faceting variables. It works best when there are two discrete variables and all their combinations appear in the data.

ggplot(data= exam_data, aes(x=MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=30) +
  facet_grid(~ GENDER)

title: 01: A Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot2 methods
section: 10 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: Coordinates
text:
10 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: Coordinates
The coordinate functions determine how data values are translated into positions on the plotting plane. ggplot2 provides several coordinate systems, each suited to different visual needs. The main ones are:

coord_cartesian(): the default Cartesian coordinate system, where you specify x and y values (e.g. allows you to zoom in or out).
coord_flip(): a Cartesian system with the x and y flipped.
coord_fixed(): a Cartesian system with a “fixed” aspect ratio (e.g. 1.78 for a “widescreen” plot).
coord_quickmap(): a coordinate system that approximates a good aspect ratio for maps.


10.1 Working with Coordinates
By default, a bar chart is displayed with the x-axis on the horizontal direction and the bars extending vertically upward, as shown in the example below.

ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x=RACE)) + geom_bar()







The code chunk below flips the x-axis to y-axis.

ggplot(exam_data, aes(x=RACE)) + geom_bar() + coord_flip()








10.2 Chaning the y-axis and x-axis Range
The scatterplot appears slightly off-centre because the axes start at different minimum values. In this case, the y-axis starts at 20, while the x-axis starts at 0, so the plotting area is not symmetric around the origin.
This happens when ggplot2 automatically sets axis limits based on the range of the data rather than forcing both axes to start at the same value. As a result, the visual centre of the plot shifts, even though the data points themselves are correctly positioned.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x= MATHS, y=ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method=lm, size=0.5)







coord_cartesian() function is used to realign the axes so they starting from 0 to 100.

ggplot(exam_data, aes(x=MATHS, y=ENGLISH)) +
        geom_point() +
        geom_smooth(method=lm, size = 0.5) +
        coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0,100), ylim= c(0,100))







Adding an additional coordinate system replaces the existing one.

ggplot(exam_data, aes(x=MATHS, y=ENGLISH)) +
        geom_point() +
        geom_smooth(method=lm, size = 0.5) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0,100), ylim= c(0,100)) +
        coord_fixed(ratio=0.8)

title: 01: A Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot2 methods
section: 11 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: themes
text:
11 Essential Grammatical Elements in ggplot2: themes
Themes control the appearance of a graph rather than the data itself, such as background colour, fonts, gridlines, and label colours.
ggplot2 includes built in themes like theme_grey() (default), theme_bw(), and theme_classic(). Theme elements are grouped into lines, rectangles, and text.

11.1 Working wth themes
theme_grey() is the default theme with background colour in grey.

ggplot(exam_data, aes(x= RACE)) +
  geom_bar() +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_grey()







The colour theme could be changed to classic where background in white and gridlines removed by using theme_classic().

ggplot(exam_data, aes(x = RACE, fill = GENDER)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_classic()







Or the theme can be set to minimal.

exam_data %>%
  count(GENDER, ENGLISH)%>%
  mutate(n = ifelse(GENDER== "Male", -n, n)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = ENGLISH, y = n, fill = GENDER)) +
  geom_col(width = 1) + 
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_y_continuous(label=abs)







Or the theme can be set to light.

ggplot(exam_data, aes(x=RACE, y =MATHS)) + 
  geom_boxplot() + 
  stat_summary(geom="point",
               fun =mean,
               shape = 21,
               fill = "red",
               colour= "black", size =3) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "text",
               aes(label = round(..y.., 0)),
               hjust = -0.5, size = 3) +

  coord_flip() +
  theme_light()







Or the theme can be set to test.

ggplot(exam_data, aes(x=CLASS,fill=RACE)) + 
  geom_bar() +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette="Paired") +
  theme_test()

2 Getting Started

2.1 Installing and Loading the Required Libraries
There are five packages that will be used in this exercise.


Package
Description



tidyverse
A collection of R packages for data importing, cleaning, transformation, and visualisation (e.g., readr, dplyr, tidyr, ggplot2).


ggrepel
Provides geoms for non-overlapping text labels in ggplot2


ggthemes
Provides ggplot2 themes, geoms and scales that replicate the famous styles ( e.g. Tufte, Economist, Tufte)


hrbrthemes
Provides minimal and professional looking themes and better typography and styleing


patchwork
Extends ggplot2 by letting user combine plots easily using operators.



The code below installs and loads the required packages into R environment. hrbrthemes package can be installed using the remote package, the code can be found on its github ReadMe.

pacman::p_load(tidyverse, ggrepel, ggthemes, hrbrthemes, patchwork)

The code chunk below solves the system warning when using hrbthemes on Windows.

extrafont::loadfonts(device = "win")
sysfonts::font_add_google("Roboto Condensed", "Roboto Condensed")
showtext::showtext_auto()


2.2 Importing the Data
A CSV file containing the final exam results of 322 local Primary 3 students has been imported into the R environment by using function read_csv() from readr package, one of tidyverse family. The dataset includes variables such as student ID, class, gender, race, and grades for English, Maths, and Science.

exam_data <- read_csv("data/Exam_data.csv")

title: 02 Beyond ggplot2 Fundamentals
text:
3 Beyond ggplot2 Annotation: ggrepel
To visualise the Maths and English scores for each student in a scatterplot, we can use geom_point() and geom_smooth() to add a reference line. However since all the student IDs are shown on the chart, the labels overlap and become difficult to read.


The plot
The code














ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x= MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
         geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(method = lm, size = 0.5) +
  geom_label(aes(label = ID, hjust = 0.5, vjust= -0.5)) + 
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0,100), ylim = c(0,100)) +
  ggtitle("English scores VS Math scores for Primary 3")




Here we could use functions like geom_text_repel() or geom_label_repel() from ggrepel package to customise the label geoms for ggplot2. The difference is that geom_label_repel() adds a rectangle behind the text, which helps the labels stand out from the background, similar to geom_label() vs geom_text() that it shows plain text only.

3.1 Working with ggrepel
ggrepel automatically places labels nicely to minimise overlap. However, we can still force all labels to be displayed by using the argument max.overlaps = Inf. The text font can be adjusted using the family argument, while the font style can be changed using fontface. In addition,box.padding controls the spacing between labels, the smaller the value, the closer the labels will be.


The plot - label
The code - label
The plot - text
The code - text














ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x= MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
         geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(method = lm, size = 0.5) +
  geom_label_repel(aes(label = ID, fontface = "bold")) + 
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0,100), ylim = c(0,100)) +
  ggtitle("English scores VS Math scores for Primary 3")














ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x= MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
         geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(method = lm, size = 0.5) +
   geom_text_repel(aes(label = ID), 
                  family = "serif", box.padding = 0.5)+
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0,100), ylim = c(0,100)) +
  ggtitle("English scores VS Math scores for Primary 3")

4.2 Working with hrbthemes Package
hrbthemes provides typographic themes and components for ggplot2 e.g. themes(theme_ipsum()), scales (scale_y_percent()), palettes(ft_cols()), fonts(font_ps()), Bit12 colour scales (scale_fill_bit12_continuous()), Flexoki palettes (flexoki_light()), utilities (flush_ticks()).


theme_ipsum()
theme_ipsum() with Styling




VIEW CODEggplot(data = exam_data, aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, boundary = 100,
                 colour = "grey25", fill = "grey90") +
  ggtitle("Distribution of Maths Scores")+
   theme_ipsum()









The hrbrthemes package has two main goals: improving typography in plots (such as label placement and fonts) and supporting efficient production workflows.
A production workflow refers to creating visuals for publication, such as blog posts, papers, reports, or presentations. While rough plots are useful during analysis, polished final graphics can help capture attention and improve audience engagement.

VIEW CODEggplot(data = exam_data, aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, boundary = 100, color="grey25", 
                 fill="grey90") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Maths Scores", caption = "Primary 3 students' year-end scores") +
  theme_ipsum(axis_title_size = 18,
              base_size = 15,
              grid = "Y")
















TipTips




axis_title_size controls the axis title font size
base_size Sets the default text size for the theme
grid Controls whether grid lines appear. If set to “Y”, it shows grid lines mainly to help track values along the y-axis (making it easier to compare heights/levels).
base_family is used to set the font family. On Windows, the default fonts used by theme_ipsum() (Arial Narrow) and theme_ft_rc() (Roboto Condensed) may not be installed, which causes warning messages. If base_family is not specified, R will fall back to the default sans font. However, we can use font_import() from extrafont package to import the fonts from system fonts folder to a R font database (the process might take a few minutes) and then load the fonts into the R environment by using loadfonts(device = "win"). Alternatively, we use font_add_google() from sysfonts package to download the fonts and load the fonts using showtext_auto() from showtext package.

5 Beyond Single Graph
We usually need multiple graphs to tell a compelling visual story. Several ggplot2 extensions provide functions for composing figures made up of multiple plots. In this section, we learn how to create a composite plot by combining multiple graphs. First, let us create three statistical graphics using the code chunk below.


p1
p2
p3




VIEW CODEp1<- ggplot(data = exam_data,
            aes(x=MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, boundary = 100,
                 colour = "grey25", fill = "grey90") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0,100)) + 
  ggtitle("Distribution of Maths Scores")

p1










VIEW CODEp2<- ggplot(data = exam_data,
            aes(x=ENGLISH)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, boundary = 100,
                 colour = "grey25", fill = "grey90") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0,100)) + 
  ggtitle("Distribution of English Scores")

p2










VIEW CODEp3<- ggplot(data = exam_data,
            aes(x=MATHS, y =ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = lm, linewidth= 0.5) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0,100), ylim = c(0,100)) + 
  ggtitle("English Scores versus Maths Scores for Primary 3")

p3











5.1 Creating Composite Graphics: pathwork Methods
Several ggplot2 extension packages support composite figures, such as grid.arrange() from gridExtra package and plot_grid() from cowplot. In this section, we learn patchwork, a ggplot2 extension designed to combine multiple ggplot2 plots into one figure.

Patchwork has a simple syntax:




+ arranges plots side by side





() groups plots





/ stacks plots vertically



5.2 Combining Two ggplot2 Graphs
The tabset below shows two histograms combined using patchwork by using +. The syntax is simple and intuitive.


Left & right
Top & bottom




VIEW CODEp1 + p2










VIEW CODEp1 / p2











5.3 Combining Three ggplot2 Graphs
More complex composite plots can be created using patchwork operators. For example, the figure below uses / to stack plots, | to place plots side by side, and () to control the layout order.
Further examples can be found on plot Assembly.


Three graphs
Graph with table




VIEW CODE(p1 / p2) | p3









Here, wrap_table() from patchwork is used to create a table. A similar result can also be achieved using gt() from the gt package.

VIEW CODEp3 + wrap_table(exam_data[1:10, c("MATHS", "ENGLISH")], panel = "full", space = "fixed") 











5.4 Creating a Composite Figure with Tag
To help reference subplots in the text, patchwork also supports auto-tagging, as shown in the figure below. Auto-tagging can be enabled by setting tag_levels in plot_annotation() to specify the tag style: '1' for Arabic numerals, 'A' for uppercase letters, 'a' for lowercase letters, 'I' for uppercase Roman numerals, and 'i' for lowercase Roman numerals.


Simple tagging
Tag with prefix and suffix




VIEW CODE((p1 / p2) | p3) +
  plot_annotation(
    tag_levels = "I",
    caption = "Disclaimer: These plots are mainly for practice.")










VIEW CODE((p1 / p2) | p3) + plot_annotation(tag_levels = c('A', '1'), tag_prefix = 'Fig. ',
                                 tag_sep = '.', tag_suffix = ':',caption = "Disclaimer: These plots are mainly for practice.")











5.5 Creating Figure with Insert
Besides arranging plots using predefined layouts, we could use inset_element() from pacthwork to place one or more plots or graphical elements freely on top of, or within, another plot.






TipKey arguments for inset_element()




p: object to inset (ggplot/grob/gt/etc.)
left, bottom, right, top: inset position (numeric or unit)
align_to: reference area (“panel” (default), “plot”, “full”)
on_top: place inset above or below the main plot
clip: clip inset to bounds or not
ignore_tag: exclude inset from auto-tagging





Basic use
Alignment
Tagging



Tip: keep values between 0 and 1 (npc units) and always ensure left < right, bottom < top.

VIEW CODEp3 + inset_element(p2, 
                   left = 0.02, 
                   bottom = 0.7, 
                   right = 0.5, 
                   top = 1)










VIEW CODEp3 + inset_element(p2, 
                   left = 0.5, 
                   bottom = 0.05, 
                   right = 1, 
                   top = 0.3,
                   align_to = "plot")










VIEW CODEp3 + inset_element(p2, 0.5, 0.05, 1, 0.3, align_to= "plot",ignore_tag= TRUE) +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = '1',  caption = "Demenstration only")











5.6 Creating a Composite Figure by Using patchwork and ggtheme


ggthemes
Built-in themes
hrbthemes



Figure below is created by combining patchwork and theme_economist() of ggthemes package using operator &, applying to all plots in the patchwork layout. If you use + , the theme is applied only to the last patchwork object, not every subplot.

VIEW CODEpatchwork <- p3 / (p1 + p2) 
patchwork & theme_economist()










VIEW CODEpatchwork <- (p1 / p2) | p3
patchwork & theme_linedraw() 










VIEW CODEpatchwork <- (p1 / p2) | p3
patchwork  & theme_modern_rc(grid="Y")
